Question: Teams \(A\) and \(B\) are playing a series of games. If either team has an equal chance to win any game, and Team \(A\) must win two games while Team \(B\) must win three games to win the series, then the odds favoring Team \(A\) to win the series are:
Solution:
Method 1: Count outcomes of four games

Assume the games are independent and each team wins each game with probability \(1/2\), the conventional interpretation of this problem. The series must be decided within four games: if A has not won twice by then, B has won at least three times.

Imagine recording four game outcomes even if the series ends earlier. This gives \(2^4=16\) equally likely outcome sequences, each with probability \(1/16\). Continuing the record does not change the series winner.

A wins the series exactly when at least two of the four outcomes are A wins. Indeed, in that case there are at most two B wins, so B cannot have reached three first. If there are at most one A win, B reaches three wins first.

It is shorter to count the sequences in which A loses. There is one with no A wins, and four with exactly one A win, according to its position. These cases are disjoint and include every losing sequence. Thus B wins in 5 of the 16 sequences, and A wins in the other 11. Odds in favor compare winning probability with losing probability, so
\[
P(A):P(B)=\frac{11}{16}:\frac{5}{16}=11:5.
\]

The independence qualification matters if the wording means only that each game's separate win probabilities are equal. For example, choose the first game's winner fairly, force the second game to have the opposite winner, and use independent fair games afterward. Each game is marginally fair, but after two games each team has one win. A then loses only if B wins both of the next two games, giving A probability \(3/4\) and odds \(3:1\).

Therefore choice A, \(11\) to \(5\), follows under the independent fair-game interpretation; marginal fairness alone is insufficient.

Method 2: Count the possible stopping sequences

Assume successive games are independent and fair. Write A or B for the winner of each game. For A to win the series, the final game must be its second win. Before that final game, B can have won zero, one, or two games; three B wins would already have ended the series.

With zero B wins, the only sequence is \(AA\), with probability \(1/4\).

With one B win, the sequences are \(ABA\) and \(BAA\). Each has probability \(1/8\).

With two B wins, the sequences are \(ABBA\), \(BABA\), and \(BBAA\). Each has probability \(1/16\). To see that this list is complete, the final A is fixed, and the earlier A can occupy any one of the first three positions.

These cases cover every possible A victory and are disjoint because they have different stopping sequences. Their probabilities give
\[
P(A)=\frac14+2\left(\frac18\right)
+3\left(\frac1{16}\right)=\frac{11}{16}.
\]
Since exactly one team wins the series, \(P(B)=5/16\). The odds favoring A are therefore \(11:5\).

This conclusion depends on the fair-game interpretation including independence, or equivalently fairness after every possible history. If instead the first two winners are forced to be opposite, with the first winner chosen fairly and later games independent and fair, each game's marginal probabilities remain equal. After two games A needs one more win and B needs two; A then has probability \(3/4\), giving different odds of \(3:1\).

Thus the independent fair-game model gives \(11\) to \(5\), choice A; separate equal win probabilities alone do not fix the answer.
